questions.question: State the Brundtland definition of sustainable development, and explain the three market failures that cause a free market to damage the environment, illustrating each with an example.
questions.expected_answer: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — resting on economic, social and environmental legs, with nature treated as capital rather than free income. Failure one: externalities — a tannery or kiln discharging into a river imposes real, rand-denominated costs (boiled water, lost fishing, clinic visits) on people outside its transactions, so its private cost sits below the social cost, its product is underpriced and overproduced; pollution is the market working on incomplete prices. Failure two: public goods — clean air and a stable climate are non-excludable and non-rival, so no firm can sell them, and everyone is tempted to free ride on others' restraint, as when a village collection for a cleaner chimney never fills because non-payers would breathe the same air. Failure three: missing property rights, the tragedy of the commons — an unowned abalone bed or fish stock is raced to depletion because each harvester correctly reasons that whatever they spare another will take; what everybody owns, nobody protects. Together they yield the policy logic: make invisible costs visible, price the unpriced, and give the ownerless an owner or a rule.

questions.question: Compare command-and-control measures with market-based measures for protecting the environment, giving South African examples of each, and state the mixing rule a strong evaluation should end on.
questions.expected_answer: Command and control regulates directly: emission standards, environmental impact assessments before mines and developments, zoning that protects wetlands, protected areas, and quotas such as fishing quotas and water-use licences. Strengths: certainty and enforceability where danger is acute — what kills is banned, not taxed. Weaknesses: inspection is costly, a fixed standard rewards nobody for beating the minimum, and a uniform rule ignores that compliance costs differ hugely across firms. Market-based measures write the missing price so the polluter pays: South Africa's carbon tax (in force since 2019, Africa's first) prices each ton of carbon dioxide, and the plastic-bag and tyre levies work the same way at the till — once the social cost is inside the price, every firm saves money continuously by polluting less, with no inspector required. Subsidies reverse the sign: solar water heater rebates and the renewable procurement programme that has built wind and solar capacity. Tradable permits cap total pollution and let firms trade allowances — the cap guarantees the outcome while trading finds the cheapest cuts, as in Europe's emissions trading scheme. Property rights give the commons a defender, as with community conservancies whose wildlife funds local services, and programmes like Working for Water pair restoration with jobs. The mixing rule: commands set the floor, prices move the average — ban what kills, tax what harms, cap what must be capped, and give owners to what can be owned.

questions.question: Trace the ladder of international environmental agreements from Montreal to the recent climate summits, contrasting the designs of Kyoto and Paris, and explain what South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership adds to the story.
questions.expected_answer: Montreal, 1987: the world agreed to phase out ozone-destroying CFCs; substitutes were found and the ozone layer is healing — the most successful environmental treaty and the proof that cooperation is possible. Rio, 1992: the Earth Summit produced Agenda 21, the Convention on Biological Diversity and the UNFCCC, the parent climate treaty, with its principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Kyoto, 1997: the first binding, quantified emission cuts, but only for developed countries — the United States never ratified and fast-growing emitters carried no targets, teaching that binding-for-some cannot bend a global curve. Johannesburg, 2002: the World Summit on Sustainable Development linked environment to poverty, water and energy access. Paris, 2015: nearly every nation submits nationally determined contributions — self-set targets that must tighten over time — aiming to hold warming well below two degrees while pursuing one and a half; universal where Kyoto was partial, voluntary where Kyoto was binding, which is at once its strength and its weakness. The recent summits added a coal phase-down agreement (Glasgow, 2021, which also finalised carbon-market rules), the loss-and-damage fund (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022), and the first global stocktake calling for a transition away from fossil fuels (Dubai, 2023). The JETP, announced at Glasgow, pledges 8,5 billion dollars from wealthy nations to help coal-dependent South Africa decarbonise justly — retraining coal workers and diversifying coal towns — carrying sustainability's social leg into energy policy.
